`sort` now has `-s` (`--stable`) and `-u` (`--unique`), and both work with `-n` and `-k` the way GNU's do. `printf '1\n01\n' | sort -nu` prints just `1`. The tests pass.

- **`-u` compares only what you sort by.** With `-n`, lines with the same number count as duplicates, and with `-k` only the keys are compared. Plain `-u` with no `-n` or `-k` removes only identical lines. Of each group of duplicates, the one that came first in the input is kept, as in GNU.
- **`-s` stops the byte-by-byte tiebreak.** Normally, lines whose keys tie are then ordered by their full text; with `-s` they stay in input order instead.

I compared 8000 random inputs and option sets (now including `-s` and `-u`) against GNU sort 9.4, plus your `1`/`01` case and the other spot checks I ran. All matched.

One thing that may surprise you, and it's how GNU behaves too: a key with its own option ignores the global `-r`. So in `sort -t: -k2,2n -ru` the `-r` does nothing. Write `-k2,2nr -u` instead. Two of my first tests assumed otherwise; GNU's output showed the code was right, so I fixed the tests.

The changes are in `cmd/sort/main.go`, `cmd/sort/main_test.go` and the README, and aren't committed. The `cut -b`/`-c` work from last time was committed between turns, but I didn't make that commit.
